title: Redundancy, Wordiness & Irrelevance
intro: Keep the meaning. Cut words that add nothing.

sections.heading: Spotting redundancy
body: Remove words that repeat meaning already present: A.M. in the morning, returned back, or combined together.
Check the full sentence, not just neighboring words. Cut only when the needed meaning and grammar remain.

examples.text: At 7 A.M. the runners gathered at the start.
examples.label: A.M. already means morning

examples.text: At 7 A.M. in the morning the runners gathered at the start.
examples.label: 'in the morning' repeats A.M.

sections.tip: Ask whether the words add meaning needed here. A repeated idea may be removable, while a time, contrast, or degree word can carry a real distinction.

sections.heading: Cutting wordiness
body: Prefer a shorter equivalent: due to the fact that → because; in order to → to; at this point in time → now; has the ability to → can.
Length alone does not decide. The shorter version must preserve the sentence’s meaning and grammatical structure.

examples.text: She left early because of the storm.
examples.label: 'because of' is tight

examples.text: She left early due to the fact that there was a storm.
examples.label: padded with empty phrasing

sections.tip: Compare a wordy phrase with a shorter equivalent, but preserve its logical role and any needed emphasis. A phrase is removable because it adds nothing here, not because its wording is always forbidden.

sections.heading: When DELETE is an option
body: Try the sentence without the underlined words. DELETE works when no needed meaning or grammatical part disappears.
If the cut removes information the paragraph needs, choose the most concise version that keeps it. If it removes the main verb or required subject, it creates a fragment.

examples.text: The museum, which is a building, opened in 1920.
examples.label: 'which is a building' adds nothing

sections.tip: Test deletion in the full sentence. Keep the cut only when the remaining grammar, necessary meaning, focus, and tone still satisfy the question.

sections.heading: Cutting irrelevant detail
body: Keep details that serve the paragraph’s purpose. A true or vivid fact can still be irrelevant.
Name the main point, then test the detail’s contribution. Choose concise wording that keeps the necessary connection.

examples.text: The chef trained in Lyon for six years before opening her own restaurant.
examples.label: every detail serves the topic

examples.text: The chef trained in Lyon, a city with many old bridges, for six years.
examples.label: the bridges are off topic

sections.tip: If a detail does not push the paragraph's main point forward, it does not belong. Interesting is not the same as relevant.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: Look for choices with similar meaning but different lengths, repeated ideas, or an OMIT/DELETE option.
Test deletion and the shortest plausible choice. Keep it only if the full sentence stays grammatical, clear, and complete in meaning.
sections.tip: When choices preserve the same meaning and grammar, prefer the concise one. NO CHANGE can be correct even for a long underline.

sections.heading: Advanced transfer: redundancy across a paragraph
body: A detail can repeat an earlier sentence even if the words differ. Compare its contribution with the whole paragraph, then retain any new contrast, condition, or limitation.

The shortest option can distort a finding by removing who was studied, the comparison, or the degree of certainty. Cut repeated wording while preserving those facts; an efficient sentence can still need a qualifying phrase.

examples.text: The survey included only registered participants. Their average travel time fell by six minutes.
examples.label: The second sentence adds the result without repeating the sample restriction.

examples.text: The survey included only registered participants. The registered participants who had registered for the survey were included.
examples.label: The second sentence restates the sample without supplying a new result.

sections.tip: Before cutting, name the new information and the qualification that must survive.

check.stem: The committee will [[reconvene again]] next week to finish the budget review.
check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most concise without losing meaning?
check.explanation: The prefix re- in 'reconvene' already means again, so 'reconvene' alone says everything the sentence needs. 'Reconvene again,' 'reconvene once more,' and 'meet again to reconvene' each repeat the idea of meeting another time.

check.stem: The machine can restart [[in the event that]] the backup battery has enough charge.
choices: on the condition that it is the case that
check.explanation: If states the condition directly and preserves the subject and finite verb of the following clause. The other choices express the same condition with unnecessary phrasing. The word before the clause must express a condition, not the reason or result in the worked example.

check.stem: The astronomer studied distant galaxies[[, and she also enjoyed gardening,]] for over thirty years.
check.questionText: Which choice best maintains the focus of the sentence?
check.explanation: The sentence is about the astronomer's research, so her gardening is off topic no matter how it is phrased. Omitting the underlined portion leaves a clean, complete sentence: 'The astronomer studied distant galaxies for over thirty years.' The choices mentioning 'gardening' all keep the irrelevant detail.
